chem_ocrb.5.1.summary: This topic covers the fundamental chemistry of acids and alkalis, focusing on the role of hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions in aqueous solutions. Students must master the distinction between strong and weak acids based on degree of ionisation, as well as the difference between concentration and strength. Furthermore, quantitative relationships involving hydrogen ion concentration and pH scales require precise mathematical and chemical understanding.

core.p: Acids are chemical substances that dissolve in water to produce hydrogen ions, H+(aq). Bases are substances that neutralise acids, and soluble bases are called alkalis.
bullets: Acids produce H+(aq) ions in water
Bases neutralise acids (e.g. metal oxides, metal hydroxides)
Alkalis are soluble bases that produce OH-(aq) ions in water
Neutralisation involves H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)

callouts.p: A substance that produces hydrogen ions, H+(aq), in aqueous solution.
A substance that reacts with an acid to form salt and water only.

core.p: The pH scale is a numerical measure from 0 to 14 of the acidity or alkalinity of an aqueous solution, measured using universal indicator or a pH probe.
bullets: pH 0 to 6 indicates an acidic solution (red, orange, yellow)
pH 7 indicates a neutral solution (green)
pH 8 to 14 indicates an alkaline solution (blue, purple)
Lower pH values correspond to higher concentrations of hydrogen ions

callouts.p: pH 7 is neutral at room temperature, representing equal concentrations of H+ and OH- ions.

core.h: C6.1 Strong Acids vs Weak Acids
core.p: Acids can be classified as strong or weak depending on how fully they ionise when dissolved in water.
bullets: Strong acids completely ionise in water (e.g. HCl, HNO3, H2SO4)
Weak acids only partially ionise in water (e.g. ethanoic, citric, carbonic acid)
Ionisation of weak acids is a reversible reaction reaching dynamic equilibrium
Strong acids have a higher concentration of H+ ions than weak acids of the same concentration

callouts.p: An acid that is completely ionised in aqueous solution.
An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution.

core.p: Concentration and strength are two completely different chemical properties that students frequently confuse.
bullets: Concentration measures the amount of acid moles dissolved in a given volume of water (e.g. mol/dm3)
Dilute acids have a low number of moles of acid per unit volume
Concentrated acids have a high number of moles of acid per unit volume
A strong acid can be dilute, and a weak acid can be concentrated

callouts.p: Never use strong to mean concentrated or weak to mean dilute. Strength is about ionisation percentage; concentration is about particles per volume.

core.h: C6.1 Hydrogen Ion Concentration and pH
core.p: The pH of a solution is directly related to the concentration of hydrogen ions present in the solution.
bullets: As the hydrogen ion concentration [H+] increases by a factor of 10, the pH decreases by 1 unit
A pH change of 2 units represents a 100-fold (10 x 10) change in [H+] concentration
Mathematically, pH = -log10[H+] (Higher tier only)
Acidic solutions have high [H+], neutral solutions have moderate [H+], alkaline solutions have very low [H+]

callouts.p: Each decrease of 1 on the pH scale means the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.

core.h: C6.1 Strong vs Weak Acid Reactions
core.p: Because strong acids have a much higher concentration of hydrogen ions than weak acids of the same concentration, their observable reaction rates differ.
bullets: Strong acids react faster with metals, metal oxides, hydroxides and carbonates
Gas evolution (e.g. hydrogen or carbon dioxide) is faster with strong acids
Temperature change during neutralisation is greater for strong acids
Total volume of gas produced is the same if moles of acid reacting are equal

callouts.p: If a weak acid reacts with magnesium, the rate of bubbling is slower, but the total volume of hydrogen gas collected is identical to a strong acid if concentrations and volumes are matched.

core.p: Neutralisation is the reaction between hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions to form water.
bullets: General equation: Acid + Base -> Salt + Water
Ionic equation: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)
Salts formed depend on the acid used (hydrochloride -> chloride, sulfuric -> sulfate)
Energy is released during neutralisation, making it an exothermic reaction

callouts.p: The reaction between the hydrogen ions in an acid and the hydroxide ions in an alkali to form water.

core.p: Experimental techniques allow us to determine both the pH and the concentration of acid solutions accurately.
bullets: Universal indicator gives an approximate pH value via colour matching
pH meters give precise, digital pH readings to several decimal places
Titrations determine the exact concentration of an acid or alkali solution
Indicator colour changes sharply at the end-point of a neutralisation titration

callouts.p: pH meters are more accurate than universal indicator because they remove human error in colour matching.

core.h: C6.1 Ethanoic Acid vs Hydrochloric Acid
core.p: Comparing ethanoic acid (weak) and hydrochloric acid (strong) illustrates the practical consequences of ionisation.
bullets: 0.1 mol/dm3 HCl has a pH of around 1 because it is fully ionised
0.1 mol/dm3 CH3COOH has a pH of around 3 because it is only partially ionised
Electrical conductivity is higher in HCl because it has many more mobile ions
Titration with sodium hydroxide requires the same total volume of NaOH for equal moles of acid

callouts.p: An organic weak acid found in vinegar, formula CH3COOH.

core.p: Higher tier students must be able to calculate changes in hydrogen ion concentration when pH changes.
bullets: If pH decreases from 3 to 1, the [H+] increases by 10 x 10 = 100 times
If pH increases from 2 to 5, the [H+] decreases by 10 x 10 x 10 = 1000 times
Use scaling factors of 10 for each single pH unit shift
Ensure proper units of mol/dm3 are stated in calculations

callouts.p: Remember: pH drop = H+ concentration increase. Think opposite directions!

core.h: C6.1 Ionic Product of Water and pH Context
core.p: In all aqueous solutions at room temperature, the product of hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations is constant.
bullets: Pure water undergoes slight self-ionisation: H2O <-> H+ + OH-
In neutral solutions, [H+] = [OH-] = 10^-7 mol/dm3, giving pH 7
In strong alkalis, [OH-] is high, so [H+] is extremely low (e.g. 10^-14)

callouts.p: Water contains tiny amounts of H+ and OH- ions due to self-ionisation.

core.h: C6.1 Experimental Evidence for Acid Strength
core.p: Simple experiments distinguish between strong and weak acids in a school laboratory.
bullets: Measuring pH with a pH meter reveals a higher pH for weak acids at equal concentration
Measuring electrical conductivity shows strong acids conduct electricity well (bright bulb)
Weak acids conduct poorly (dim bulb) due to fewer free ions
Measuring rate of reaction with magnesium ribbon shows faster hydrogen evolution with strong acids

callouts.p: Concentrated strong acids are corrosive; always wear safety goggles and handle with care in a fume cupboard if required.

analogy.t: The Crowd and the VIP Lounge
analogy.p: Imagine an acid is a concert venue where hydrogen ions are energetic fans. In a strong acid, 100% of the fans rush straight onto the dance floor (complete ionisation), creating high activity and high energy. In a weak acid, only a small fraction of the fans leave the seating area to enter the dance floor, while the rest stay seated together as molecules (partial ionisation). Concentration represents how crowded the entire venue is overall, whereas strength represents how eager the fans are to get onto the dance floor. Where the analogy breaks down is that ionisation in weak acids is a dynamic equilibrium where fans constantly move back and forth between seated and dancing states, whereas concert fans usually stay put.

mistakes.w: Saying a weak acid has a low concentration
mistakes.r: Weakness refers to partial ionisation, not concentration. A weak acid can be concentrated.

mistakes.w: Saying a strong acid has a high concentration
mistakes.r: Strength is about ionisation percentage, not how many moles are dissolved per dm3.

mistakes.w: Writing pH as PH or ph
mistakes.r: It must always be written with a lowercase 'p' and uppercase 'H' (pH).

mistakes.w: Stating pH 7 is the only neutral value at all temperatures
mistakes.r: pH 7 is neutral at 25C; neutrality means [H+] equals [OH-], which can occur at different pH values at other temperatures.

mistakes.w: Assuming weak acids don't react with reactive metals
mistakes.r: Weak acids do react with metals like magnesium, but the rate of reaction is slower than with strong acids.

mistakes.w: Believing pH scale ends at 0 and 14
mistakes.r: Extremely concentrated strong acids can have negative pH values, and concentrated alkalis can exceed pH 14.

mistakes.w: Confusing hydrogen ions with hydroxide ions
mistakes.r: Acids produce H+ ions, whereas alkalis produce OH- ions.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid in terms of ionisation.
model: Strong acids are completely ionised in aqueous solution.
Weak acids are only partially ionised in aqueous solution.
exam.tip: Mention complete versus partial ionisation to secure both marks.

exam.q: Explain why hydrochloric acid has a higher pH than a solution of ethanoic acid of the same concentration.
model: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid and completely ionised.
Ethanoic acid is a weak acid and only partially ionised.
Therefore, hydrochloric acid has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions, resulting in a lower pH.
exam.tip: Link acid strength to hydrogen ion concentration and then to pH.

exam.q: Calculate the factor by which the hydrogen ion concentration increases when the pH decreases from 4 to 2.
model: Each decrease of 1 pH unit increases [H+] by a factor of 10.
A decrease of 2 pH units increases [H+] by 10 x 10 = 100 times.
exam.tip: Show your working by breaking the step down unit by unit.

exam.q: A student states that dilute hydrochloric acid is a weak acid. Explain why this statement is incorrect.
model: Dilute describes a low concentration of acid particles in a given volume.
Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid because it completely ionises regardless of its concentration.
exam.tip: Distinguish clearly between concentration terms (dilute) and strength terms (strong).

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for neutralisation.
model: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)
exam.tip: Include state symbols if requested by the question.

exam.q: Compare the rate of reaction of 1.0 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid and 1.0 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid with excess magnesium ribbon.
model: Hydrochloric acid reacts faster than ethanoic acid.
Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid with a higher [H+] concentration.
Ethanoic acid is a weak acid with a lower [H+] concentration.
Therefore, hydrogen gas is evolved more rapidly with hydrochloric acid.
exam.tip: Reference [H+] concentration differences to explain reaction rate differences.

exam.q: Define the term 'alkali'.
model: A soluble base that produces hydroxide ions, OH-(aq), in aqueous solution.
exam.tip: Make sure to mention both solubility and hydroxide ions.

exam.q: Describe how you would experimentally distinguish between a strong acid and a weak acid of the same concentration.
model: Measure the pH using a pH meter or universal indicator.
The strong acid will have a significantly lower pH than the weak acid.
Alternatively, measure electrical conductivity or reaction rate with magnesium.
exam.tip: Give a clear experimental method and expected observation.

exam.q: Explain what happens to the hydrogen ion concentration when the pH of a solution increases from 3 to 5.
model: The hydrogen ion concentration decreases.
It decreases by a factor of 100 (10 x 10).
exam.tip: Remember that an increase in pH means a decrease in hydrogen ion concentration.

exam.q: Explain why pure ethanoic acid does not conduct electricity, but aqueous ethanoic acid does.
model: Pure ethanoic acid is molecular and contains no free ions.
When dissolved in water, it partially ionises to form mobile H+ and CH3COO- ions.
These mobile ions allow charge to flow, conducting electricity.
exam.tip: Mention mobile ions for electrical conductivity.

worked.q: Calculate the change in hydrogen ion concentration when the pH of a solution changes from 5 to 1.
steps: Identify the total change in pH units: 5 - 1 = 4 pH units.
Recall that each unit decrease in pH represents a 10-fold increase in [H+].
Calculate the overall factor: 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10,000.
worked.ans: The hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10,000.

worked.q: A solution has a hydrogen ion concentration of 0.001 mol/dm3. What is its pH?
steps: Express 0.001 in standard form: 1 x 10^-3 mol/dm3.
Recall the definition of pH: pH = -log10[H+].
Substitute the concentration: -log10(10^-3) = 3.

chem_ocrb.5.3.summary: Catalysts are substances that speed up chemical reactions without being used up themselves, achieved by lowering the activation energy through an alternative reaction pathway. Enzymes are biological catalysts made of protein molecules that work best at specific temperatures and pH levels, operating with high specificity via the lock and key mechanism. Understanding activation energy profiles and how catalysts affect them is vital for explaining industrial processes and biological systems alike.

core.p: A catalyst is a chemical substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being chemically changed or used up at the end of the reaction.
bullets: Catalysts remain chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
They are not used up, meaning a small amount of catalyst can convert a very large amount of reactant into product.
Catalysts do not change the overall energy change (Delta H) of the reaction.
They do not alter the position of equilibrium in reversible reactions, they only help the system reach equilibrium faster.

callouts.p: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction and is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
Students often state that catalysts 'are not involved' in the reaction. This is false! They take part in the reaction mechanism but are regenerated by the end.

core.p: Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that colliding particles must have in order for a chemical reaction to take place.
bullets: Represented by the symbol Ea.
Reactions with high activation energies are very slow at room temperature because few particles have enough energy when they collide.
On a reaction profile diagram, activation energy is measured from the energy level of the reactants up to the highest point of the curve (the transition state or peak).
A catalyst works by providing an alternative reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy.

callouts.p: The minimum amount of energy required for particles to react upon collision.
Always state that a catalyst provides an 'alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy', not just that it 'lowers activation energy'.

core.h: 3. How Catalysts Work on a Particle Level
core.p: By lowering the activation energy, a catalyst increases the proportion of particles that have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
bullets: When reactant particles collide in the presence of a catalyst, more collisions are successful.
Successful collisions lead to a higher rate of reaction, meaning more product is formed per unit of time.
Heterogeneous catalysts are in a different phase or state from the reactants (e.g., solid catalyst in gaseous reactants).
Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase or state as the reactants (e.g., dissolved enzymes in an aqueous solution).

callouts.p: When asked how a catalyst increases rate, state: 'It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more colliding particles have energy greater than or equal to activation energy, increasing successful collision frequency.'

core.p: Enzymes are biological catalysts made of large protein molecules folded into complex 3D shapes, which speed up metabolic reactions in living organisms.
bullets: Enzymes are highly specific: each enzyme usually only catalyzes one specific reaction or type of reaction.
They work best under specific conditions known as optimum temperature and optimum pH.
Enzymes are crucial for digestion, respiration, and DNA replication in living cells.
Like industrial catalysts, they are not used up during the reactions they catalyze.

callouts.p: A biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up biochemical reactions in living organisms.

core.p: The specificity of enzymes is explained by the lock and key model, which describes how the enzyme and its substrate fit together precisely.
bullets: The **active site** is a specialized region on the enzyme molecule with a unique shape that complements the shape of the substrate molecule.
The **substrate** is the reactant molecule that binds to the enzyme's active site.
When the substrate fits into the active site, an enzyme-substrate complex is temporarily formed.
The reaction takes place rapidly, products are released, and the enzyme remains unchanged and ready to bind with another substrate molecule.

callouts.p: The shape of the active site is complementary to only one specific substrate. If the substrate shape does not match, no reaction occurs.

core.h: 6. Effect of Temperature on Enzyme Activity
core.p: Temperature affects enzyme activity by altering kinetic energy and molecular collision frequency, up to a critical point where denaturation occurs.
bullets: As temperature increases from low values, enzyme and substrate particles move faster and collide more frequently, increasing the rate.
The **optimum temperature** is the temperature at which the enzyme works at its maximum possible rate (typically around 37°C in humans).
Above the optimum temperature, excessive thermal energy causes the protein structure to vibrate violently.
This breaks the bonds holding the 3D shape together, permanently changing the shape of the active site so the substrate no longer fits. This process is called **denaturation**.

callouts.p: Enzymes are molecules, not living things. They cannot be 'killed'. Always state that they are **denatured**.

core.h: 7. Effect of pH on Enzyme Activity
core.p: Changes in pH alter the electrical charges on the amino acid groups that make up the active site, disrupting ionic bonds and tertiary structure.
bullets: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which its active site has the precise shape required for maximum catalytic activity.
For example, pepsin (stomach protease) works best in strongly acidic conditions (pH 2), whereas salivary amylase works near neutral (pH 7).
If the pH becomes too high or too low compared to the optimum, the bonds holding the active site's structure together are broken.
This results in denaturation of the enzyme, rendering it completely inactive as substrates can no longer bind.

callouts.p: The permanent loss of catalytic activity caused by the change in shape of the active site, following the disruption of internal bonds by extreme temperature or pH.

core.p: Enzymes are widely used in commercial and industrial processes because they operate under mild conditions, saving energy and money.
bullets: **Biological washing powders**: contain proteases and lipases to break down protein and fat stains (food, blood) at lower wash temperatures.
**Food industry**: isomerase converts glucose syrup into fructose syrup, which is sweeter and used in smaller quantities.
**Brewing and baking**: carbohydrases break down starch into sugars for fermentation by yeast.
**Advantages**: operate at room temperature and normal pressure, reducing energy costs and high-pressure equipment requirements.

callouts.p: Always remember: enzymes save money because they work at lower temperatures and pressures, requiring less energy input.

core.p: Despite their efficiency, enzymes have several drawbacks that limit their use in certain chemical manufacturing plants.
bullets: They are easily denatured by small changes in temperature or pH, requiring strict and expensive environmental controls.
It can be difficult and expensive to separate the enzyme from the reaction mixture once the process is complete.
Enzymes can be expensive to produce in large quantities using microorganisms.
They can be inhibited by trace contaminants or heavy metal ions present in industrial feedstocks.

callouts.p: Do not say enzymes are always cheap. While they save energy costs, making and purifying specific enzymes for industrial reactors can be very expensive.

core.p: Many industrial chemical processes use transition metals or their compounds as heterogeneous catalysts to speed up reactions.
bullets: **Iron (Fe)** is used as a catalyst in the Haber process for manufacturing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
**Platinum (Pt) / Rhodium (Rh)** are used as catalysts in catalytic converters in cars to convert toxic gases into harmless ones.
**Nickel (Ni)** is used to catalyze the hydrogenation of alkenes (adding hydrogen to vegetable oils to make margarine).
These catalysts provide active sites on their surfaces where reactant molecules can adsorb, react, and then desorb.

callouts.p: Transition metals are exceptional catalysts because they can change oxidation states and provide surface adsorption sites.

analogy.t: The Lock, Key, and Master Matchmaker Analogy
analogy.p: Imagine an enzyme is like a custom-built lock (the active site) and the substrate is the specific key that fits it. When the key is inserted, it easily turns (the reaction occurs) and pops open the door, leaving the lock ready for the next key. A catalyst overall is like a matchmaker who introduces two people who are too shy to meet on their own (lowering the barrier to interaction) without getting married to either of them. Where this breaks down: real enzymes and substrates undergo slight conformational shifts (induced fit), and human matchmakers do get tired, whereas catalysts process millions of cycles without degradation.

terms.d: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or chemically changed.
The minimum energy required by colliding particles for a reaction to occur.
A biological catalyst, made of protein, that speeds up metabolic reactions in living organisms.
The specific region on an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
The reactant molecule that fits into the enzyme's active site during a biochemical reaction.
The permanent change in the 3D shape of an enzyme's active site caused by extreme heat or pH, stopping function.
The temperature at which an enzyme works at its fastest rate.
The pH value at which an enzyme exhibits maximum catalytic activity.
The temporary structure formed when a substrate molecule is bound to the enzyme's active site.
A catalyst that is in a different physical state or phase from the reactants.
A catalyst that is in the same physical state or phase as the reactants.
A block of elements in the periodic table frequently used as industrial catalysts due to their variable oxidation states.

mistakes.w: Catalysts make reactions happen that otherwise would never occur.
mistakes.r: Catalysts only speed up reactions that are already thermodynamically possible; they do not start impossible reactions.

mistakes.w: Catalysts are used up during the reaction.
mistakes.r: Catalysts participate in the reaction mechanism but are regenerated completely by the end.

mistakes.w: Enzymes are killed by high temperatures.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are molecules, not living organisms, so they are denatured, not killed.

mistakes.w: A catalyst lowers the activation energy by increasing particle speed.
mistakes.r: Temperature increases particle speed. A catalyst lowers activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway.

mistakes.w: Enzymes work at any temperature as long as it is hot enough.
mistakes.r: Enzymes have an optimum temperature; above this, they denature and rate drops to zero.

mistakes.w: The active site changes shape to fit any substrate.
mistakes.r: The active site is specific; it has a complementary shape to only one specific substrate.

mistakes.w: Catalysts change the amount of product made.
mistakes.r: Catalysts only change how fast the reaction reaches completion; they do not increase the final yield of products.

exam.q: Define the term 'activation energy'.
model: The minimum energy required for particles to react upon collision.
exam.tip: Learn this exact definition word for word to secure the mark.

exam.q: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction.
model: Provides an alternative reaction pathway
with a lower activation energy
so more particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy, increasing successful collision frequency.
exam.tip: Include all three marking points: alternative pathway, lower activation energy, and proportion of successful collisions.

exam.q: Describe what happens to an enzyme when it is heated above its optimum temperature.
model: Excess thermal energy breaks bonds holding the protein structure
changing the 3D shape of the active site
so the substrate no longer fits (enzyme is denatured).
exam.tip: Make sure to use the word 'denatured' and explain that the active site shape changes.

exam.q: State the catalyst used in the Haber process.
model: Iron
exam.tip: You can write iron or Fe.

exam.q: Explain why biological washing powders containing enzymes are more economical for washing clothes at 30°C than traditional detergents at 90°C.
model: Enzymes work effectively at lower temperatures
which reduces the energy required to heat the water, saving money.
exam.tip: Link lower temperature to energy savings.

exam.q: Draw and label a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction with and without a catalyst.
model: Axes labelled Energy and Progress of reaction
Reactants higher than products for exothermic
Uncatalyzed peak higher than catalyzed peak
Activation energy labelled clearly for both pathways
exam.tip: Ensure the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants for an exothermic reaction profile.

exam.q: Explain why enzymes are specific in terms of the lock and key model.
model: The active site has a specific 3D shape
which is complementary to only one specific substrate molecule
so other substrates cannot fit into the active site.
exam.tip: Use the words 'complementary' and 'active site'.

exam.q: Give two advantages of using enzymes in industrial processes.
model: Operate at lower temperatures and pressures reducing energy costs
They are specific, meaning fewer unwanted side products.
exam.tip: Keep points concise and distinct.

exam.q: Explain why changing the pH away from the optimum pH decreases enzyme activity.
model: Changes in hydrogen ion concentration alter internal charges
disrupting bonds that hold the active site structure
causing the enzyme to denature.
exam.tip: Mention bond disruption and denaturation.

worked.q: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the rate of starch breakdown by amylase. At 20°C, the reaction takes 120 seconds. At 30°C, it takes 60 seconds. Calculate the rate of reaction at 30°C taking rate as 1 / time.
steps: Identify the formula: Rate = 1 / time
Substitute the values for 30°C: Rate = 1 / 60
Calculate the final value: 0.0167 s^-1

worked.q: Explain how a catalyst affects the energy changes during a reversible reaction at equilibrium.
steps: Recall that catalysts speed up both the forward and reverse reactions equally.
State that the overall energy change (Delta H) remains unchanged.
Conclude that the position of equilibrium is unchanged, but is reached faster.
worked.ans: The catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions by the same factor, so Delta H and the equilibrium position are unchanged, but equilibrium is reached faster.

chem_ocrb.5.5.summary: These top-tier revision notes cover OCR GCSE Chemistry B specification point C6.3 on reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium. They provide a comprehensive breakdown of how reactions can go in both directions, the conditions required for a closed system, and the characteristics of dynamic equilibrium. Designed for grade 9 students, the notes include clear SVG diagrams, precise terminology, common exam pitfalls, and worked examples to secure top marks.

core.p: Some chemical reactions can proceed in both the forward and backward directions. These are called **reversible reactions** and are represented in chemical equations using a double arrow instead of a single forward arrow.
bullets: The **forward reaction** is when reactants turn into products.
The **backward reaction** is when products turn back into reactants.
If a reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic by the exact same energy change in the reverse direction.
An example is the thermal decomposition of hydrated copper(II) sulfate into anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water.

callouts.p: A reaction in which the conversion of reactants to products and the conversion of products to reactants occur simultaneously.

core.p: For a reversible reaction to reach a state of **dynamic equilibrium**, it must take place inside a **closed system**. This ensures that no reactants or products can escape or enter the surroundings.
bullets: In an **open system**, gases can escape into the atmosphere, meaning the reverse reaction cannot happen and equilibrium cannot be established.
A closed system traps all participating chemical species so they remain available to react.
Examples of closed systems include a sealed flask or a stoppered test tube.
Temperature must also be kept constant to prevent shifts driven by external thermal changes.

callouts.p: Students often forget to mention that a closed system prevents escape of gases. Without this, a reverse reaction cannot occur for gaseous products.

core.p: When a reversible reaction is in **dynamic equilibrium**, the macroscopic properties (like colour and pressure) appear constant, but microscopic activity continues unabated at the molecular level.
bullets: **Dynamic** means the reactions are still actively occurring in both directions.
**Equilibrium** means the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction.
Concentrations of all reactants and products remain constant over time.
There is no macroscopic change visible to the observer once equilibrium is reached.

callouts.p: The state reached in a closed system when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction.

core.h: 4. Rate of Forward and Backward Reactions
core.p: At the start of a reaction (time zero), the rate of the forward reaction is at its maximum because reactant concentration is highest. As reactants are used up, the forward rate decreases.
bullets: Initially, the rate of the backward reaction is zero because there are no products.
As products form, the rate of the backward reaction increases.
Eventually, the decreasing forward rate and the increasing backward rate become equal.
Once the rates are equal, the system has reached dynamic equilibrium.

callouts.p: At equilibrium, rates are equal. Concentrations are NOT necessarily equal; they are just constant.

core.p: The **position of equilibrium** tells us the relative amounts of reactants and products present when the system is at equilibrium.
bullets: If the position lies **to the right**, there are more products than reactants at equilibrium.
If the position lies **to the left**, there are more reactants than products at equilibrium.
Changing conditions (like temperature, pressure, or concentration) can alter the position of equilibrium.
Catalysts do not change the position of equilibrium; they only help the system reach equilibrium faster.

callouts.p: Never confuse the position of equilibrium (amounts) with the rate of reaction (how fast it gets there).

core.h: 6. Reversible Thermal Decomposition of Ammonium Chloride
core.p: Ammonium chloride is a classic example of a reversible thermal decomposition reaction used to demonstrate dynamic equilibrium in a sealed tube.
bullets: Equation: NH4Cl(s) <==> NH3(g) + HCl(g).
When heated at the bottom of a test tube, solid ammonium chloride breaks down into colourless ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases.
As the gases rise and cool near the top of the tube, they react together to reform solid ammonium chloride.
This creates a white ring of solid further up the tube in a closed setup.

callouts.p: Endothermic in the forward direction, exothermic in the reverse direction.

core.p: Another standard school demonstration of reversibility involves the colour change between hydrated and anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
bullets: Equation: CuSO4.5H2O(s) <==> CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l).
Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is bright blue.
When heated strongly, water is driven off, leaving white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
Adding water back to the anhydrous solid releases heat and immediately turns it blue again.

callouts.p: Containing water molecules chemically combined within the crystal structure.

core.p: Exam questions often present graphs showing how concentration or rate changes over time until equilibrium is established.
bullets: On a **rate-time graph**, equilibrium is reached when the forward and backward rate lines merge into a single horizontal line.
On a **concentration-time graph**, equilibrium is reached when the separate reactant and product curves flatten out and become parallel to the x-axis.
The point where the curves flatten marks the onset of dynamic equilibrium.
Steepness of the initial curve indicates how fast the reaction starts.

callouts.p: Make sure you state that concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal, when looking at a flat concentration-time graph.

core.p: Adding a catalyst to a reversible system has specific effects on both the forward and backward reactions without disturbing the final yields.
bullets: A catalyst speeds up the forward reaction and the backward reaction by the exact same factor.
Activation energy is lowered for both directions equally.
Because both rates increase equally, the position of equilibrium does not change.
The only benefit of a catalyst in an equilibrium system is that it reaches equilibrium much faster.

callouts.p: Catalysts increase rate, NOT yield. They save time and energy by cutting down the time needed to reach equilibrium.

core.p: To prove or explain that a system is in dynamic equilibrium, students must reference specific defining criteria.
bullets: The system must be closed (no matter enters or leaves).
Macroscopic properties (colour, concentration, pressure) remain constant.
Rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction.
The processes are ongoing at a microscopic level despite no overall net change.

callouts.p: A system isolated from its surroundings so that no matter can be transferred in or out.

analogy.p: Imagine people walking up a downward-moving escalator at a shopping centre. If 5 people walk up the stairs every minute, and exactly 5 people ride the escalator back down or walk down every minute, the total number of people on the escalator stays constant (equilibrium), even though individual people are constantly moving (dynamic). This breaks down because people have free will and do not follow strict mathematical rates like molecules reacting according to collision theory.

terms.d: A reaction where products can react to reform the original reactants.
State in a closed system where forward and backward reaction rates are equal.
A system where no substances can enter or leave.
Reaction where reactants form products.
Reaction where products form reactants.
The relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium.
Containing chemically bonded water of crystallization.
Containing no water molecules.
Substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
Minimum energy needed for particles to react.
Properties observable with the naked eye, such as colour or pressure.
At the level of individual atoms and molecules.

mistakes.w: Saying equilibrium means the amounts of reactants and products are equal.
mistakes.r: Equilibrium means the RATES of forward and backward reactions are equal, and concentrations are CONSTANT, not necessarily equal.

mistakes.w: Stating that reactions stop when equilibrium is reached.
mistakes.r: Reactions do not stop; both forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates (dynamic).

mistakes.w: Forgetting to mention a closed system.
mistakes.r: Always state that the reaction must be in a closed system for equilibrium to occur.

mistakes.w: Believing a catalyst increases the yield of a reversible reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst only increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached, leaving the yield unchanged.

mistakes.w: Using a single arrow for a reversible reaction.
mistakes.r: Must use a double half-arrow (<==>) symbol for reversible reactions.

mistakes.w: Confusing rate with position of equilibrium.
mistakes.r: Rate is how fast a reaction goes; position of equilibrium is the relative amounts of substances present.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a 'closed system' in the context of a reversible reaction.
model: A system where no matter or substances can escape
or enter from the surroundings.
exam.tip: Always mention that reactants and products cannot leave or enter.

exam.q: Describe what happens to the rates of the forward and backward reactions as a reversible reaction approaches equilibrium starting from pure reactants.
model: Rate of forward reaction decreases as reactants are used up
Rate of backward reaction increases as products are formed
Eventually both rates become equal at equilibrium
exam.tip: Mention both directions and how their rates change over time.

exam.q: State two features of a reaction that is in dynamic equilibrium.
model: Rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction
Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant
exam.tip: Learn these two core conditions word for word.

exam.q: A student heats hydrated copper(II) sulfate in an open test tube and claims it is a reversible reaction in dynamic equilibrium. Explain why the student is incorrect.
model: The test tube is open, allowing water vapour to escape
This means it is not a closed system
Therefore the reverse reaction cannot occur and equilibrium cannot be reached
exam.tip: Link the open tube to the escape of gas and failure to form equilibrium.

exam.q: Explain why adding a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
model: It increases the rate of both the forward and backward reactions by the same amount
Therefore the relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium remain unchanged
exam.tip: Emphasise that both rates are affected equally.

exam.q: Define the term 'dynamic equilibrium'.
model: In a closed system, the rate of the forward reaction equals
the rate of the backward reaction.
exam.tip: Make sure to include 'closed system' and equal rates.

exam.q: What type of arrow is used in chemical equations to represent a reversible reaction?
model: A double arrow (<==>)
exam.tip: Draw clear opposing half-arrows.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of the forward reaction decreases over time in a closed system.
model: Reactants are used up as they turn into products
So there are fewer reactant particles per unit volume leading to fewer successful collisions
exam.tip: Link particle frequency to decreasing reactant concentration.

exam.q: Describe the colour change seen when water is added to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
model: Changes from white
to blue
exam.tip: Mention start and end colours in order.

worked.q: A reaction mixture containing gases A and B reaches dynamic equilibrium to form gases C and D in a closed container. Sketch and explain how the rates of the forward and backward reactions change from the start until equilibrium is reached.
steps: Identify initial state: At time zero, pure reactants (A and B) are present, so forward rate is maximum and backward rate is zero.
Describe changes over time: As A and B react, their concentration falls, so forward rate decreases. As C and D form, backward rate increases.
Identify equilibrium: Eventually, the decreasing forward rate and increasing backward rate meet and become equal.
worked.ans: The forward rate starts high and decreases over time. The backward rate starts at zero and increases over time. Equilibrium is established when the two rates intersect and become equal, running parallel thereafter.

worked.q: Explain why solid ammonium chloride can form a white ring at the top of a heated test tube during thermal decomposition.
steps: Thermal decomposition: Solid ammonium chloride absorbs heat near the bottom of the tube to form ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases.
Transport of gases: The gases diffuse upwards into the cooler upper regions of the test tube.
Reverse reaction: In the cooler zone, the reverse reaction takes place, combining ammonia and hydrogen chloride to reform solid ammonium chloride.
worked.ans: Ammonium chloride decomposes upon heating into gases at the bottom. As these gases rise into the cooler upper regions of the closed tube, they recombine in the reverse exothermic reaction to form solid ammonium chloride as a white ring.

chem_ocrb.5.6.summary: This topic covers how dynamic equilibria respond to changes in external conditions such as concentration, temperature, and pressure, as predicted by Le Chatelier's principle. Understanding these shifts allows chemists to select compromise conditions in industrial processes like the Haber process to balance reaction rate and position of equilibrium. Mastering these concepts is essential for explaining how reversible reactions adjust to minimise imposed stress.

core.p: When a reversible reaction is at dynamic equilibrium and you change the conditions, the system shifts to counteract that change. This fundamental rule of chemical systems allows us to predict how the yields of products will change when temperature, pressure, or concentration are altered.
bullets: Applies strictly to systems in closed containers at dynamic equilibrium.
States that if a stress is applied to a system, the position of equilibrium shifts to counteract the effect of the stress.
Stresses include changes in concentration, temperature, or total pressure.
Helps industrial chemists maximize yield and economic viability.

callouts.p: If a stress is applied to a system at dynamic equilibrium, the system shifts to counteract that stress.
Equilibrium can only be established and shifted in a closed system where reactants and products cannot escape.

core.p: Altering the concentration of reactants or products forces the equilibrium to shift to use up the added substance or replace the removed substance.
bullets: If reactant concentration is increased, the equilibrium shifts to the right to make more products.
If product concentration is increased, the equilibrium shifts to the left to make more reactants.
If a product is continuously removed (e.g. condensed to a liquid), the equilibrium shifts to the right to produce more product, increasing overall yield.
Concentration changes do not alter the value of the equilibrium constant, only the position.

callouts.p: Continuously removing products prevents the reverse reaction from occurring effectively, driving forward yield to 100%.

core.p: Temperature changes affect reversible reactions differently depending on whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
bullets: An increase in temperature shifts the equilibrium in the **endothermic** (positive enthalpy change, +ΔH) direction.
A decrease in temperature shifts the equilibrium in the **exothermic** (negative enthalpy change, -ΔH) direction.
If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature decreases the yield of products.
Temperature is unique because it alters both the position of equilibrium AND the rate of reaction simultaneously.

callouts.p: Think of heat as a reactant in endothermic reactions and a product in exothermic reactions.

core.p: Pressure changes only affect equilibria involving gases. The system responds by shifting towards the side with fewer or more moles of gas molecules.
bullets: Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with **fewer moles of gas**.
Decreasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with **more moles of gas**.
If there are equal moles of gas on both sides of the equation (e.g. H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)), changes in pressure have **no effect** on the position of equilibrium.
High pressures increase the rate of reaction because particles are closer together, colliding more frequently.

callouts.p: Only count big stoichiometric numbers in front of gaseous species ((g)), ignore (s), (l), and (aq).

core.p: Catalysts increase the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions equally by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
bullets: A catalyst has **no effect** on the position of equilibrium.
It does not change the yield of products at equilibrium.
It simply helps the system reach dynamic equilibrium **much faster**.
Crucial in industrial processes to save time and energy costs.

callouts.p: Speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally without being used up.

core.h: Choosing Industrial Conditions: Rate vs Yield
core.p: Industrial chemists must balance chemical theory (Le Chatelier's principle and collision theory) with economic reality to choose the best operating conditions.
bullets: High pressure gives high yield (if fewer moles of product) and fast rate, but requires extremely expensive, thick-walled steel pipes and high electrical pumping costs.
Low temperature gives high yield (if forward reaction is exothermic), but the reaction rate becomes dangerously slow, making the process uneconomical.
A **compromise condition** is selected to give a reasonable yield at a reasonable rate in an acceptable time frame.
Unreacted gases are usually recycled back into the reactor to maximize overall efficiency.

callouts.p: Max yield does not equal max profit if energy costs or reaction times are too high.

core.p: The Haber process manufactures ammonia (NH3) from nitrogen and hydrogen gases for use in fertilizers. The reaction is reversible and exothermic.
bullets: Equation: N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) (-ΔH = exothermic).
Total moles of gas: 4 moles on the left, 2 moles on the right.

core.p: A classic lab demonstration of a reversible reaction involves the hydration and dehydration of copper(II) sulfate crystals.
bullets: Equation: CuSO4.5H2O(s) <=> CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l).
Forward reaction (adding water) is exothermic and turns white anhydrous copper sulfate blue.
Reverse reaction (heating) is endothermic, turning blue hydrated copper sulfate white and driving off water.
Demonstrates how temperature changes shift equilibrium between hydrated and anhydrous forms.

core.h: Effect of Concentration Changes: Iodine Clock & Chromate/Dichromate
core.p: Chromate and dichromate ions in aqueous solution provide a vivid colour change demonstration of shifting equilibrium via concentration changes.
bullets: Equation: 2CrO42-(yellow) + 2H+(aq) <=> Cr2O72-(orange) + H2O(l).
Adding acid (increasing [H+]) shifts the equilibrium to the right, turning the solution from yellow to orange.
Adding alkali (decreasing [H+] by reacting with H+ ions) shifts the equilibrium to the left, turning the solution from orange to yellow.
Demonstrates direct application of Le Chatelier's principle with ionic species in solution.

callouts.p: Adding H+ shifts equilibrium away from the added species to consume it.

core.p: In processes like the Haber process, single-pass conversion rates of reactants to products can be low (e.g., around 15%). Recycling ensures high overall efficiency and zero raw material waste.
bullets: Gasses leaving the reactor are cooled so that ammonia liquefies and is separated out.
Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gases are recycled back through the compressor and heater into the reactor vessel.
Overall conversion efficiency approaches 98% due to this continuous loop.
Saves raw materials and reduces industrial operating costs.

callouts.p: Recycling ensures that low single-pass yields do not result in wasted reactants.

analogy.p: Imagine a shopping mall escalator where people are walking up from the ground floor to the top floor at the exact same rate that people are walking back down the stairs. If more people suddenly crowd onto the bottom floor (increasing reactant concentration), more people will start walking up to clear the crowd (shift right). If the mall management turns up the heat and people get sluggish (temperature change), the rate slows down. This breaks down because chemical particles do not make conscious choices to move; instead, particle collision probabilities dictate the shifts.

mistakes.w: A catalyst shifts the equilibrium to the right to make more product.
mistakes.r: A catalyst increases the rate of both forward and reverse reactions equally, so it has NO effect on the position of equilibrium.

mistakes.w: Increasing pressure always increases the yield of products.
mistakes.r: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with FEWER moles of gas. If both sides have equal moles, pressure has no effect on yield.

mistakes.w: Raising the temperature always increases product yield in reversible reactions.
mistakes.r: Raising temperature only increases yield for endothermic forward reactions. For exothermic reactions, raising temperature decreases yield.

mistakes.w: Equilibrium stops when the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
mistakes.r: Equilibrium means rates are equal, not concentrations. Concentrations remain constant, but are rarely equal.

mistakes.w: Le Chatelier's principle says the system stops the change completely.
mistakes.r: The system 'partially opposes' or 'counteracts' the change, it never completely cancels out the imposed stress.

mistakes.w: In the Haber process, high temperature gives maximum yield.
mistakes.r: High temperature gives a faster rate, but a lower yield because the forward reaction is exothermic.

mistakes.w: Pressure changes affect aqueous solutions and solids in equilibrium.
mistakes.r: Pressure changes only affect gases because liquids and solids are virtually incompressible.

exam.q: State Le Chatelier's principle.
model: If a stress is applied to a system at dynamic equilibrium
the system shifts to counteract that stress.
exam.tip: Learn this definition word for word to secure both marks easily.

exam.q: The forward reaction in the Haber process is exothermic. Explain why a compromise temperature of 450 C is used instead of a very low temperature.
model: A lower temperature would give a higher yield because the forward reaction is exothermic
However, a lower temperature makes the rate of reaction too slow
450 C provides a compromise
It gives a reasonable yield at an acceptable reaction rate for economic viability.
exam.tip: Always link temperature choices to both rate and yield arguments in industry.

exam.q: Consider the gaseous equilibrium: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g) (-Delta H). Predict and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the position of equilibrium.
model: Equilibrium shifts to the right
There are 3 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles of gas on the right
The system shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas to reduce pressure.
exam.tip: Count the stoichiometric coefficients carefully before writing your answer.

exam.q: Describe the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of equilibrium.
model: No effect on the position of equilibrium.
exam.tip: Do not fall into the trap of saying catalysts increase yield.

exam.q: Explain why unreacted gases are recycled in the Haber process.
model: Single-pass conversion is low / not all reactants turn into products
Recycling ensures high overall efficiency and prevents waste of raw materials.
exam.tip: Mention raw material conservation and economic efficiency.

exam.q: In the equilibrium: A(g) + 2B(g) <=> 3C(g), state what happens to the equilibrium yield of C if the concentration of A is increased.
model: Yield of C increases
Equilibrium shifts to the right to use up the added reactant A.
exam.tip: Always specify the direction of the shift alongside the yield change.

exam.q: Explain how hydrated copper sulfate can be turned into anhydrous copper sulfate.
model: Heat the hydrated copper sulfate
Water is driven off as steam, leaving white anhydrous copper sulfate behind.
exam.tip: State both the action (heating) and the observation (colour change / steam).

exam.q: Why must a system be closed for dynamic equilibrium to be established?
model: So that reactants and products cannot escape
Allowing both forward and reverse reactions to occur continuously at equal rates.
exam.tip: Make sure to mention containment of gases or volatile substances.

exam.q: Predict the effect of decreasing temperature on an endothermic forward reaction.
model: Equilibrium shifts to the left
Yield of products decreases.
exam.tip: Trace enthalpy signs carefully: endothermic +Delta H absorbs heat.

exam.q: Suggest why very high pressures (e.g. 1000 atmospheres) are not used in the Haber process.
model: Requires extremely expensive thick-walled reaction vessels
High electrical energy costs for pumping gases, making it economically unviable.
exam.tip: Industrial questions often test economic factors like equipment and energy costs.

worked.q: A gaseous equilibrium is represented by: X(g) + 2Y(g) <=> 2Z(g) (+Delta H). Explain what adjustments to temperature and pressure should be made to obtain the maximum possible yield of Z.
steps: Analyze the enthalpy change for temperature: The forward reaction is endothermic (+Delta H).
Apply Le Chatelier's principle for temperature: Increasing the temperature will shift the equilibrium to the right (endothermic direction), increasing the yield of Z.
Count moles of gas for pressure: Left side has 1 + 2 = 3 moles of gas. Right side has 2 moles of gas.
Apply Le Chatelier's principle for pressure: Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas (the right side), increasing the yield of Z.
worked.ans: To obtain the maximum yield of Z, high temperature and high pressure should be applied.

worked.q: The reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) has a negative enthalpy change. A student claims that lowering the temperature to 100 C and raising the pressure to 500 atm is the best way to run this industrial process. Evaluate this claim using chemical principles.
steps: Evaluate temperature: Since the forward reaction is exothermic, 100 C would give a very high yield of ammonia. However, low temperature results in an extremely slow reaction rate.

Evaluate pressure: 500 atm would shift equilibrium to the right (fewer moles of gas) and increase reaction rate, but high pressure requires extremely expensive, robust equipment and high pumping costs.
Evaluate student claim: While chemical yield would be high, the process would be uneconomical due to extremely slow reaction times at 100 C and prohibitive equipment costs at 500 atm.
Conclusion: Compromise conditions (450 C and 200 atm) are used instead to balance rate, yield, and economic cost.
worked.ans: The student's claim is incorrect economically; compromise conditions are necessary because low temperature makes the rate too slow and high pressure is too expensive.

chem_ocrb.5.9.summary: Atom economy is a theoretical measure of how efficiently reactant atoms are converted into desired products in a chemical reaction, directly impacting industrial sustainability and raw material conservation. Choosing optimal reaction pathways requires balancing high atom economy, high percentage yield, fast rates, and favourable equilibrium positions. Sustainable chemistry demands minimising waste, using renewable resources, and recycling by-products to reduce environmental footprints and economic costs.

core.h: 1. Definition and Significance of Atom Economy
core.p: Atom economy is a crucial metric in green chemistry that quantifies the proportion of reactant atoms that actually end up in the desired product. In industrial chemistry, maximizing atom economy reduces chemical waste, conserves finite natural resources, and decreases disposal costs. A low atom economy means many atoms are wasted as unwanted by-products, which creates hazardous waste streams and reduces overall process efficiency.
bullets: Calculated using masses from the balanced chemical equation
Focuses entirely on the stoichiometry of desired versus total products
Higher atom economy means fewer waste products and greener chemistry
Crucial for evaluating the commercial and environmental viability of industrial routes

callouts.p: The percentage of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product, calculated by dividing the relative formula mass of the desired product by the sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants, multiplied by 100.

core.p: To calculate atom economy, you must use the balanced chemical equation, find the relative formula masses (Mr) of all reactants, and compare the Mr of the desired product to the total Mr of all reactants. Stoichiometric coefficients (big numbers) must be included in the calculation because they account for all moles of substances reacting and forming. Even if a reaction has a 100 percent percentage yield, its atom economy might be very low if large amounts of unwanted by-products are formed.
bullets: Formula: (Mr of desired product / Total Mr of all reactants) * 100
Always multiply individual Mr values by their stoichiometric coefficients
Units cancel out because atom economy is expressed as a percentage
Addition of all reactant masses equals the addition of all product masses (law of conservation of mass)

callouts.p: Always multiply the Mr of a substance by its balancing number in the chemical equation before calculating atom economy.

core.p: Addition reactions occur when two or more reactant molecules combine to form a single product molecule. Because all reactant atoms are incorporated into the single product, there are no waste by-products generated. Consequently, addition reactions always have an atom economy of exactly 100 percent. This makes them extremely desirable in industrial chemistry for maximizing efficiency and eliminating the need for complex waste separation and disposal systems.
bullets: All reactant atoms end up in the desired product
No atoms are left over or converted into waste by-products
Atom economy is always 100 percent for addition processes
Examples include the hydrogenation of alkenes and polymerisation reactions

callouts.p: A reaction where two or more molecules react together to form a single larger molecule, resulting in 100 percent atom economy.

core.h: 4. Atom Economy in Substitution and Elimination Reactions
core.p: Unlike addition reactions, substitution and elimination reactions involve replacing or removing atoms, inevitably producing one or more by-products alongside the desired product. Because some reactant atoms end up in these by-products rather than the desired substance, the atom economy is always less than 100 percent. Industrial chemists must carefully evaluate whether the economic value of the desired product outweighs the financial and environmental costs of managing the waste by-products.
bullets: By-products are formed in addition to the desired product
Total mass of reactants is split between desired product and waste
Lower atom economy requires finding valuable uses for by-products
Common in organic synthesis of pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals

callouts.p: Do not confuse percentage yield (how much product you actually make compared to maximum theoretical) with atom economy (how many atoms end up in the desired product).

core.p: Industrial chemists often have multiple synthetic routes available to manufacture the same chemical product. Choosing the best pathway requires comparing both the atom economy and the percentage yield of each competing route. A pathway with a very high atom economy might still be rejected if its percentage yield is extremely low due to unfavorable equilibrium positions or difficult separation steps. Conversely, a lower atom economy pathway might be used if the by-product can be sold or reused elsewhere in the plant.
bullets: Compare atom economies of competing industrial pathways
Evaluate percentage yield alongside atom economy
Consider the toxicity and disposal costs of waste by-products
Factor in energy costs required for high temperatures and pressures

callouts.p: Chemical companies choose pathways balancing atom economy, percentage yield, reaction rate, raw material cost, and safety.

core.p: The choice of an industrial reaction pathway is heavily driven by economics, raw material availability, and production costs. Cheap raw materials are preferred, but if they lead to low atom economy or difficult waste disposal, the overall profit margin may shrink. Companies also evaluate energy requirements, such as whether a pathway needs expensive high temperatures or high pressures, which increase capital and running costs.
bullets: Cost of starting materials significantly affects economic viability
Energy costs for heating and pressurisation must be minimized
Disposal costs for hazardous waste can ruin a profitable process
Selling valuable by-products can offset the disadvantage of low atom economy

callouts.p: When asked why an industrial process is sustainable or economical, mention reducing waste, high atom economy, and reusing by-products.

core.p: Sustainable chemistry (green chemistry) aims to design chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the generation of hazardous substances. High atom economy directly contributes to sustainability by ensuring that fewer resources are extracted and less waste is released into the environment. Chemical manufacturers must also consider the carbon footprint of their energy sources and the persistence of any waste products released into ecosystems.
bullets: Minimizes depletion of finite non-renewable resources
Reduces release of toxic pollutants into air, water, and soil
Encourages use of renewable feedstocks where possible
Lowers environmental remediation and taxation costs for companies

callouts.p: Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, achieved in chemistry through waste reduction and efficient resource use.

core.p: When a reaction pathway has a low atom economy, unwanted by-products are inevitably produced. To make the process commercially viable and environmentally acceptable, chemical plants must find ways to handle this waste. The best approach is finding a secondary commercial use for the by-product, effectively turning waste into a valuable co-product. If no use can be found, the waste must be treated, neutralized, or safely disposed of without harming local ecosystems.
bullets: Convert waste into useful co-products for secondary markets
Recycle unreacted starting materials back into the reaction vessel
Treat hazardous waste chemically before safe disposal
Minimize environmental impact to comply with strict government regulations

callouts.p: The ultimate aim of green chemistry is zero waste, where all by-products are captured and repurposed.

core.p: Industrial chemists almost never achieve an ideal process where atom economy, percentage yield, reaction rate, and equilibrium position are all simultaneously at their maximum. Instead, industrial processes represent a series of carefully engineered compromises. For example, lower temperatures might give a better percentage yield in an exothermic reversible reaction, but the reaction rate would become too slow to be economically viable, requiring the use of a catalyst or higher temperatures.
bullets: Balancing high atom economy with acceptable percentage yield
Weighing fast reaction rates against equilibrium position constraints
Balancing high capital costs of equipment with long-term operating profits
Compromising operating pressure to save energy while maintaining safety

callouts.p: Never state that an industrial process has 100 percent yield and 100 percent atom economy unless it is a simple addition reaction with complete conversion.

core.h: 10. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Pathway Evaluation
core.p: A Life Cycle Assessment evaluates the environmental impact of a chemical product across its entire existence, from raw material extraction through manufacturing, packaging, transport, use, and final disposal or recycling. Atom economy is a key input into the manufacturing stage of an LCA. By improving atom economy, manufacturers reduce the environmental burden calculated in the LCA, making their products more attractive to environmentally conscious consumers and regulators.
bullets: Assesses environmental impact from cradle to grave
Includes extraction of raw materials, manufacturing, transport, and disposal
Atom economy directly affects the manufacturing phase impact score
Helps compare the true sustainability of different synthetic pathways

callouts.p: An assessment of the total environmental impact of a product throughout its entire life cycle from raw material extraction to final disposal.

core.p: Consider the industrial production of a chemical where Route A uses an addition reaction with 100 percent atom economy and 85 percent yield, while Route B uses a substitution reaction with 45 percent atom economy and 95 percent yield. Route A is generally preferred despite the slightly lower yield because it generates zero waste by-products, saving massive costs on waste separation and disposal. However, if Route B's by-product has a high market value as a separate commodity, Route B might become more economically profitable.
bullets: Route A: High atom economy (100%), moderate yield (85%), zero waste
Route B: Low atom economy (45%), high yield (95%), valuable by-product
Economic analysis determines which route yields higher net profit
Environmental regulations can tip the balance toward high atom economy routes

callouts.p: Be prepared to calculate atom economy for unfamiliar equations in exam questions using relative atomic masses provided in the data table.

analogy.p: Imagine running a bakery making decorated celebration cakes. Atom economy is like measuring how much of the flour, sugar, and butter you bought actually ends up in the final edible cake versus how much ends up as spilled batter, trimmings, and inedible waste on the floor. If you use an 'addition' recipe where every single gram of mixed ingredients forms the cake, your atom economy is 100 percent. If your recipe requires cutting off crusts or producing useless chemical scraps (substitution), your atom economy drops. The analogy breaks down because in baking, trimmings can sometimes be eaten by staff or fed to animals, whereas chemical waste often requires expensive, specialized hazardous disposal.

Designing chemical products and processes to maximize efficiency and minimize the use and generation of hazardous substances.
Meeting current human needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A reaction where two or more molecules combine to form a single product, resulting in 100 percent atom economy.
A reaction where an atom or group in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group, reducing atom economy.
A reaction where atoms are removed from a molecule, producing a smaller molecule and a by-product.
The actual amount of product obtained in a reaction compared to the maximum theoretical amount, expressed as a percentage.
An incidental or secondary product produced alongside the desired product in a chemical reaction.
An analysis of the total environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction to final disposal.
Raw materials supplied to a chemical manufacturing process to be converted into products.
The calculation of relative quantities of reactants and products in chemical reactions based on balanced equations.
A secondary product generated alongside a primary product that has commercial value and can be sold.

mistakes.w: Confusing atom economy with percentage yield.
mistakes.r: Percentage yield measures practical efficiency (how much you actually make), whereas atom economy measures theoretical atomic efficiency (how many atoms end up in the desired product).

mistakes.w: Stating that all reactions have an atom economy of 100 percent.
mistakes.r: Only addition reactions have 100 percent atom economy. Substitution and elimination reactions produce by-products, giving an atom economy of less than 100 percent.

mistakes.w: Omitting balancing numbers when calculating Mr sums.
mistakes.r: You must multiply the relative formula mass of each substance by its stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced equation.

mistakes.w: Believing that a 100 percent yield means 100 percent atom economy.
mistakes.r: You can have 100 percent yield of the desired product while still having a low atom economy because large amounts of waste by-products were formed.

mistakes.w: Saying atom economy depends on practical losses like spilled liquids.
mistakes.r: Atom economy is entirely theoretical and calculated from the balanced equation; practical losses affect percentage yield, not atom economy.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include the mass of all reactants in the denominator.
mistakes.r: The denominator must be the sum of the Mr of all substances shown reacting in the balanced equation.

mistakes.w: Assuming a low atom economy reaction is never used industrially.
mistakes.r: Low atom economy reactions are used if the percentage yield is very high, the raw materials are extremely cheap, or the by-product can be sold profitably.

exam.q: Define atom economy and explain why a high atom economy is important in industrial chemical processes.
model: Percentage of reactant atoms that end up in desired product
Reduces waste / conserves raw materials
Decreases disposal costs / more sustainable
exam.tip: Always link high atom economy to resource conservation and waste reduction for full marks.

exam.q: Calculate the atom economy for the production of iron from iron(III) oxide using carbon monoxide: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. (Relative atomic masses: Fe = 56, C = 12, O = 16).
model: Total Mr of reactants = 160 + (3*28) = 244 (or total mass of desired product = 112)
Mr of desired product (2Fe) = 2 * 56 = 112
exam.tip: Show all working clearly: calculate total reactant mass, desired product mass, and divide before multiplying by 100.

exam.q: Explain why addition reactions always have an atom economy of 100%.
model: All reactant atoms combine to form a single product
No waste by-products are formed
exam.tip: Keep the explanation concise, focusing on the combination into a single product with no left-over atoms.

exam.q: A chemical company can manufacture a medical drug using two different reaction pathways. Route A has 95% atom economy and 40% yield. Route B has 55% atom economy and 90% yield. Discuss which route is better.
model: Route A has higher atom economy, producing less waste and lower disposal costs
Route B has much higher percentage yield, meaning less reactant is wasted as unreacted material
Route A uses atoms more efficiently but low yield means losing expensive starting materials
Company must balance waste disposal costs against raw material costs to make a final decision
exam.tip: In evaluation questions, analyze both positive and negative points for each option before reaching a balanced conclusion.

exam.q: State two factors, other than atom economy and percentage yield, that chemical companies consider when choosing an industrial reaction pathway.
model: Cost of raw materials
Energy requirements / operating temperature and pressure
Rate of reaction
Marketability of by-products
exam.tip: Learn at least four industrial factors so you can select two distinct ones not mentioned in the stem.

exam.q: Explain the difference between percentage yield and atom economy.
model: Percentage yield compares actual amount of product made to theoretical maximum
Atom economy measures proportion of reactant atoms incorporated into desired product
exam.tip: Contrast practical recovery (yield) with theoretical atomic stoichiometry (atom economy).

exam.q: Why might a chemical company use a reaction pathway with an atom economy of only 35%?
model: The percentage yield is very high
The by-product can be sold for a profit as a co-product
Raw starting materials are extremely cheap
exam.tip: Mention economic drivers like valuable by-products or cheap feedstocks.

exam.q: Describe the environmental benefits of increasing atom economy in chemical manufacturing.
model: Reduces consumption of finite raw materials
Produces less hazardous waste requiring disposal
exam.tip: Focus on resource conservation and pollution reduction.

exam.q: In a manufacturing process, 50g of reactant A produces 30g of desired product B and 20g of waste C. Calculate the atom economy.
model: Desired mass = 30, Total reactant mass = 50
Atom economy = (30 / 50) * 100 = 60%
exam.tip: Check whether total mass equals reactants; here 30 + 20 = 50, so use desired mass divided by total reactant mass.

worked.q: Calculate the atom economy for making hydrogen gas by reacting zinc with hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. (Relative atomic masses: H = 1, Cl = 35.5, Zn = 65).
steps: Identify the desired product: hydrogen gas (H2) and calculate its Mr: 2 * 1 = 2.
Calculate the Mr of all reactants: Zn = 65, 2HCl = 2 * (1 + 35.5) = 73. Total reactant mass = 65 + 73 = 138.
Substitute values into the atom economy formula: (Mr of desired product / Total Mr of reactants) * 100.
Calculate percentage: (2 / 138) * 100 = 1.45%.

worked.q: Calculate the atom economy for the manufacture of ethanol by the hydration of ethene: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH. (Relative atomic masses: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16).
steps: Identify the desired product: ethanol (C2H5OH) and calculate its Mr: (2 * 12) + (6 * 1) + 16 = 46.
Calculate the Mr of all reactants: ethene (C2H4) = 28, water (H2O) = 18. Total reactant mass = 28 + 18 = 46.
Recognise that this is an addition reaction where all reactant atoms form a single product.
Substitute into formula: (46 / 46) * 100 = 100%.

worked.q: A student heats calcium carbonate to produce calcium oxide and carbon dioxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Calculate the atom economy for producing calcium oxide (CaO). (Relative atomic masses: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40).
steps: Identify desired product: CaO and calculate its Mr: 40 + 16 = 56.
Calculate total Mr of reactants: CaCO3 = 40 + 12 + (3 * 16) = 100.
Calculate atom economy: (Mr of CaO / Mr of CaCO3) * 100.
